title: Living Under Pressure: Suitable Areas for an Endangered Coastal Dolphin Overlap With Intense Human Activities
content:
ABSTRACT

Marine ecosystems, especially coastal ones, are experiencing increased pressure from human activities. The first step to develop effective and appropriate management strategies is to understand the underlying processes of species distribution. The Guiana dolphin is a threatened coastal species, vulnerable to human-induced rapid environmental change due to its proximity to anthropogenic stressors. In this study, we modelled and mapped habitat suitability for Guiana dolphins in an anthropized estuarine complex: Sepetiba–Ilha Grande bays (SB-IGB), in the Brazilian southern coast, where multiple stressors have been affecting these populations. To predict habitat suitability, we ran 750 distribution models, including five algorithms (GLM, GAM, GBM, RF and MaxEnt), and generated an ensemble model with those that achieved ROC > 0.85. We categorized suitable areas (high, medium and low) by dividing equal intervals between maximum and cut-off values. Human activities were overlapped to qualitatively evaluate exposure to stressors. Our results demonstrated that 25% of the SB-IGB complex is suitable for dolphins and they are more likely to occur in two unconnected shallow areas due to a deeper mid area. Of the suitable areas for dolphins, 90% overlapped with anthropogenic stressors, such as industrial poles, ports, anchorage areas, dredged channels and shipping routes. This highlights the relatively strict habitat limits of this species in the SB-IGB estuarine complex, where the environment is rapidly changing. The proximity and overlap between areas that are highly suitable for dolphins and those where human activities take place underscore the need for effective conservation and regulation strategies, particularly as these areas support feeding and nursing.
